claim: Insecticide-treated nets (ITNs) comprise conventional (cITNs) and long-lasting insecticidal nets (LLINs).
source: Insecticide-treated nets (ITNs), which comprise conventional (cITNs) and long-lasting insecticidal nets (LLINs), are the single most widely used intervention for malaria control in Africa, proven to significantly reduce morbidity and mortality via direct protection and community-wide reductions in transmission (Lim et al., 2011; Lengeler and Lengeler, 2004; Eisele et al., 2010; Killeen et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a definitional statement that establishes the composition of ITNs, supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: ITNs are proven to significantly reduce malaria morbidity and mortality via direct protection and community-wide reductions in transmission.
source: Insecticide-treated nets (ITNs), which comprise conventional (cITNs) and long-lasting insecticidal nets (LLINs), are the single most widely used intervention for malaria control in Africa, proven to significantly reduce morbidity and mortality via direct protection and community-wide reductions in transmission (Lim et al., 2011; Lengeler and Lengeler, 2004; Eisele et al., 2010; Killeen et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research studies.

claim: ITNs are the single most widely used intervention for malaria control in Africa.
source: Insecticide-treated nets (ITNs), which comprise conventional (cITNs) and long-lasting insecticidal nets (LLINs), are the single most widely used intervention for malaria control in Africa, proven to significantly reduce morbidity and mortality via direct protection and community-wide reductions in transmission (Lim et al., 2011; Lengeler and Lengeler, 2004; Eisele et al., 2010; Killeen et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and represents established knowledge about malaria control interventions.

claim: The World Health Organization (WHO) promotes a target of universal coverage for all populations at risk with either ITNs or indoor residual spraying (IRS).
source: The World Health Organization (WHO) promotes a target of universal coverage for all populations at risk with either ITNs or indoor residual spraying (IRS), with the former representing the primary vector control tool in nearly all endemic African countries (WHO, 2013a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to WHO documentation.

claim: ITNs represent the primary vector control tool in nearly all endemic African countries.
source: The World Health Organization (WHO) promotes a target of universal coverage for all populations at risk with either ITNs or indoor residual spraying (IRS), with the former representing the primary vector control tool in nearly all endemic African countries (WHO, 2013a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to WHO documentation.

claim: The international community has invested billions of dollars in the provision of at least 700 million LLINs since 2004.
source: The international community has invested billions of dollars in the provision of at least 700 million LLINs since 2004 (WHO, 2013a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to WHO documentation.

claim: These investments have led to enormous scale up in population access to ITNs.
source: While these investments have led to enormous scale up in population access to ITNs (Noor et al., 2009; Monasch et al., 2004), the target of universal coverage remains distant and millions of African households at risk remain unprotected (WHO, 2013a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The target of universal coverage remains distant and millions of African households at risk remain unprotected.
source: While these investments have led to enormous scale up in population access to ITNs (Noor et al., 2009; Monasch et al., 2004), the target of universal coverage remains distant and millions of African households at risk remain unprotected (WHO, 2013a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to WHO documentation.

claim: Gold standard measurements of ITN coverage indicators are provided by nationally representative household surveys such as Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS), Multiple Indicator Cluster Surveys (MICS), and Malaria Indicator Surveys (MIS).
source: Gold standard measurements of these indicators are provided by nationally representative household surveys such as Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS) (Measure, 2014), Multiple Indicator Cluster Surveys (MICS) (UNICEF, 2012), and Malaria Indicator Surveys (MIS) (RBM, 2014a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the survey programs and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Nationally representative household surveys are carried out relatively infrequently.
source: These surveys are carried out relatively infrequently, however, meaning they cannot be used directly for evaluating year-on-year coverage trends or for generating timely estimates of continent-wide coverage levels.
evidence: This is an inference based on the nature of survey implementation and its implications for monitoring.

claim: Household surveys cannot be used directly for evaluating year-on-year coverage trends or for generating timely estimates of continent-wide coverage levels.
source: These surveys are carried out relatively infrequently, however, meaning they cannot be used directly for evaluating year-on-year coverage trends or for generating timely estimates of continent-wide coverage levels.
evidence: This is an inference based on the infrequent nature of surveys.

claim: Programmatic data such as the number of ITNs delivered and distributed within countries are available for most countries and years.
source: In contrast, programmatic data such as the number of ITNs delivered and distributed within countries, while not describing coverage directly, are available for most countries and years (WHO, 2013a ).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to WHO documentation.

claim: Flaxman and colleagues used a compartmental modelling approach to link programmatic and survey data, generating annual estimates of two ITN indicators.
source: In a 2009 study, Flaxman and colleagues (Flaxman et al., 2010) used a compartmental modelling approach to link these programmatic and survey data, generating annual estimates of the two ITN indicators recommended at that time on access (% households with at least one ITN) and use (% children < 5 years old who slept under an ITN the previous night).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the Flaxman et al. study.

claim: An intra-household 'ownership gap' may exist whereby many households with some nets may not have enough for one net between two occupants.
source: An intra-household 'ownership gap' may exist whereby many households with some nets may not have enough for one net between two occupants (the recommended minimum level of protection (WHO, 2013b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to WHO guidance and represents a conceptual understanding of coverage gaps.

claim: One net between two occupants is the recommended minimum level of protection.
source: An intra-household 'ownership gap' may exist whereby many households with some nets may not have enough for one net between two occupants (the recommended minimum level of protection (WHO, 2013b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to WHO guidance.

claim: A 'usage gap' may exist whereby individuals with access to a net do not sleep under it.
source: Similarly, a 'usage gap' may exist whereby individuals with access to a net do not sleep under it.
evidence: This represents a conceptual understanding of coverage gaps based on established knowledge.

claim: The measurement of two additional ITN indicators was recommended: % households with at least one ITN for every two people and % population with access to an ITN within their household.
source: In response, the measurement of two additional indicators was recommended: % households with at least one ITN for every two people and % population with access to an ITN within their household (assuming each net was used by two people) (RBM, UNICEF, WHO, 2013; RBM, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to RBM, UNICEF, and WHO guidance documents.

claim: The indicator on usage was extended to include the entire population rather than only children under 5 years old.
source: In addition, the indicator on usage was extended to include the entire population rather than only children under 5 years old.
evidence: This represents a change in indicator definition based on established guidance.

claim: Countries have an ongoing struggle to maintain high LLIN coverage in the face of continuous loss of nets from households due to damage, repurposing, or movement away from target areas.
source: Countries have an ongoing struggle to maintain high LLIN coverage in the face of continuous loss of nets from households due to damage, repurposing, or movement away from target areas.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about challenges in maintaining ITN coverage.

claim: The rate of net loss and the degree of over-allocation of new nets play a key role in determining how efficiently delivery to countries will translate into household coverage levels.
source: Together, the rate of net loss and the degree of over-allocation of new nets play a key role in determining how efficiently delivery to countries will translate into household coverage levels.
evidence: This is an inference about the factors affecting coverage efficiency.

claim: The WHO define universal access to ITNs on the basis that two people can share one net.
source: The WHO define universal access to ITNs on the basis that two people can share one net.
evidence: This represents established WHO guidance.

claim: Using the working assumptions of a 3-year ITN lifespan and a 1.8 person-per-net ratio, a simple calculation yields an indicative estimate of 150 million new nets required each year to provide universal coverage to an African population at risk of around 810 million.
source: Using the working assumptions of a 3-year ITN lifespan and a 1.8 person-per-net ratio (one-between-two but allowing for odd-numbered households), a simple calculation yields an indicative estimate of 150 million new nets required each year to provide universal coverage to an African population at risk of around 810 million (WHO, 2013a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to WHO documentation and represents a calculation based on stated assumptions.

claim: 41 of the 47 endemic African countries have implemented the RBM-HWG needs assessment approach.
source: To support country planning and donor application processes (RBM-HWG, 2014), a more elaborate needs assessment approach has been developed by the RBM Harmonization Working Group (RBM-HWG) and implemented by 41 of the 47 endemic African countries (RBM, 2014; Paintain et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to RBM documentation.

claim: Countries have calculated a continent-wide need for 920 million ITNs over the 2014–2017 period (approximately 230 million per year).
source: Countries have used these inputs to calculate requirements for new nets to achieve national coverage targets, leading to an estimated continent-wide need for 920 million ITNs over the 2014–2017 period (approximately 230 million per year) (RBM, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to RBM documentation.

claim: Some 718 million LLINs have been delivered across the 40 endemic countries since their introduction in 2004.
source: Some 718 million LLINs have been delivered across the 40 endemic countries since their introduction in 2004.
evidence: This claim is based on data analysis presented in the study.

claim: Annual LLIN deliveries increased year-on-year from 2004 to 2010, reaching 145 million in that year.
source: As is well documented (WHO, 2013a), annual LLIN deliveries increased year-on-year from 2004 to 2010, reaching 145 million in that year, but then declined dramatically in 2011 and 2012 to less than half that amount before rising again to 143 million in 2013 (green line).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A and cited WHO documentation.

claim: LLIN deliveries declined dramatically in 2011 and 2012 to less than half the 2010 amount before rising again to 143 million in 2013.
source: As is well documented (WHO, 2013a), annual LLIN deliveries increased year-on-year from 2004 to 2010, reaching 145 million in that year, but then declined dramatically in 2011 and 2012 to less than half that amount before rising again to 143 million in 2013 (green line).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A and cited WHO documentation.

claim: There were 252 million LLINs in sub-Saharan households by the end of 2013.
source: We estimate that there were 252 million LLINs in sub-Saharan households by the end of 2013, with that net crop growing approximately linearly from 2004, with the exception of a slow-down resulting from the reduced supply of nets in 2011–2012.
evidence: This is an estimate derived from the model analysis presented in the study, shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The net crop grew approximately linearly from 2004, with the exception of a slow-down resulting from the reduced supply of nets in 2011–2012.
source: We estimate that there were 252 million LLINs in sub-Saharan households by the end of 2013, with that net crop growing approximately linearly from 2004, with the exception of a slow-down resulting from the reduced supply of nets in 2011–2012.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data analysis and model results shown in Figure 1A.

claim: cITNs constituted nearly all ITNs prior to 2005 but diminished rapidly in importance following the introduction of LLINs thereafter.
source: Figure 1B shows equivalent distribution and resulting net crop estimates for cITNs, which constituted nearly all ITNs prior to 2005 but diminished rapidly in importance following the introduction of LLINs thereafter.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: By the end of 2013, around two-thirds (66%, 95% CI 62%–71%) of households at risk owned at least one ITN.
source: By the end of 2013, we estimate that around two-thirds (66%, 95% CI 62%–71%) of households at risk owned at least one ITN.
evidence: This is an estimate derived from the model analysis, shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Less than one-third (31%, 29%–34%) of households owned enough ITNs for one ITN between two people by the end of 2013.
source: However, less than one-third (31%, 29%–34%) owned enough for one ITN between two people.
evidence: This is an estimate derived from the model analysis, shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 48% (45%–51%) of people at risk had access to an ITN within their household (on a one-between-two basis) by the end of 2013.
source: This much lower level of adequate ownership is reflected in the levels of access and use, with 48% (45%–51%) of people at risk having access to an ITN within their household (on a one-between-two basis) and 43% (39%–46%) sleeping under an ITN the previous night.
evidence: This is an estimate derived from the model analysis, shown in Figure 2C.

claim: 43% (39%–46%) of people at risk slept under an ITN the previous night by the end of 2013.
source: This much lower level of adequate ownership is reflected in the levels of access and use, with 48% (45%–51%) of people at risk having access to an ITN within their household (on a one-between-two basis) and 43% (39%–46%) sleeping under an ITN the previous night.
evidence: This is an estimate derived from the model analysis, shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The ownership gap has been narrowed from 77% (76%–78%) of net-owning households having insufficient nets in 2000 to 56% (54%–57%) in 2013.
source: Encouragingly, this gap has been narrowed from 77% (76%–78%) of net-owning households having insufficient nets in 2000 to 56% (54%–57%) in 2013.
evidence: This is an estimate derived from the model analysis, shown in Figure 2E.

claim: A large majority (89%, 84%–93%) of those with access to an ITN in the household slept under it the previous night.
source: Analysis of the 'use gap' suggested a large majority (89%, 84%–93%) of those with access to an ITN in the household slept under it the previous night, and we found no evidence of significant change in this proportion through time.
evidence: This is an estimate derived from the model analysis.

claim: There was no evidence of significant change in the proportion of those with access who slept under an ITN through time.
source: Analysis of the 'use gap' suggested a large majority (89%, 84%–93%) of those with access to an ITN in the household slept under it the previous night, and we found no evidence of significant change in this proportion through time.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: Nearly all countries began with very low coverage levels in 2000 and display a marked inflection point towards the middle of the decade.
source: Nearly all countries began with very low coverage levels in 2000 and display a marked inflection point towards the middle of the decade, although there was considerable variation in the timing of onset of concerted scale-up activities.
evidence: This is an observation based on the data shown in Figure 3.

claim: There was considerable variation in the timing of onset of concerted scale-up activities across countries.
source: Nearly all countries began with very low coverage levels in 2000 and display a marked inflection point towards the middle of the decade, although there was considerable variation in the timing of onset of concerted scale-up activities.
evidence: This is an observation based on the data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The monotonic increases in coverage seen at the aggregated continental level are often replaced at national level with pronounced periods of rise and fall.
source: Importantly, the monotonic increases in coverage seen at the aggregated continental level are often replaced at national level with pronounced periods of rise and fall, and in many cases, 2013 does not represent the peak year.
evidence: This is an observation based on the data shown in Figure 3.

claim: In many cases, 2013 does not represent the peak year for ITN coverage at the national level.
source: Importantly, the monotonic increases in coverage seen at the aggregated continental level are often replaced at national level with pronounced periods of rise and fall, and in many cases, 2013 does not represent the peak year.
evidence: This is an observation based on the data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The population with access to ITNs within the household was at or below 15% in seven countries in 2013.
source: The population with access to ITNs within the household, for example, was at or below 15% in seven countries in 2013, while above 70% for the top four.
evidence: This is an observation based on the data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The population with access to ITNs within the household was above 70% for the top four countries in 2013.
source: The population with access to ITNs within the household, for example, was at or below 15% in seven countries in 2013, while above 70% for the top four.
evidence: This is an observation based on the data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Over the 14-year period since 2000, on average 15% (12%–18%) of all ITNs distributed to households were over-allocated.
source: Over the 14-year period since 2000, on average 15% (12%–18%) of all ITNs distributed to households were over-allocated (owned by households already owning sufficient nets for one-between-two).
evidence: This is an estimate derived from the model analysis.

claim: Around 7% (6%–9%) of ITNs were over-allocated in 2000.
source: Around 7% (6%–9%) of ITNs were over-allocated in 2000, and this has risen steadily to 27% (22%–32%) in 2013.
evidence: This is an estimate derived from the model analysis, shown in Figure 4.

claim: Over-allocation has risen steadily to 27% (22%–32%) in 2013.
source: Around 7% (6%–9%) of ITNs were over-allocated in 2000, and this has risen steadily to 27% (22%–32%) in 2013.
evidence: This is an estimate derived from the model analysis, shown in Figure 4.

claim: Over-allocation increased approximately 15 percentage points for each one-ITN-per-capita increase in net crop.
source: The year-on-year increase in over-allocation is to some extent an expected consequence of the overall growth in ITN provision: we found that over-allocation increased approximately 15 percentage points for each one-ITN-per-capita increase in net crop.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: Over-allocation varied substantially between countries, ranging in 2013 from 50% (36%–65%) in the Republic of the Congo to 11% (9%–15%) in Côte D'Ivoire.
source: Over-allocation also varied substantially between countries, for example ranging in 2013 from 50% (36%–65%) in the Republic of the Congo to 11% (9%–15%) in Côte D'Ivoire.
evidence: This is an observation based on the data analysis.

claim: Averaged over all years and all countries, the median retention time for LLINs in households was 23 (20–28) months.
source: Averaged over all years and all countries, we found the median retention time for LLINs in households was 23 (20–28) months.
evidence: This is an estimate derived from the model analysis.

claim: There was no statistically significant evidence of continent-wide temporal trends in retention times.
source: We found no statistically significant evidence of continent-wide temporal trends in retention times, but substantial between-country variation.
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis.

claim: There was substantial between-country variation in LLIN retention times.
source: We found no statistically significant evidence of continent-wide temporal trends in retention times, but substantial between-country variation.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis, shown in Figure 5.

claim: Rates of loss for the first 3 years were greater than both the Flaxman et al. and RBM-HWG alternatives for all countries.
source: As can be seen, we found rates of loss for the first 3 years to be greater than both these alternatives for all countries.
evidence: This is a comparison based on the data analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Under a business-as-usual scenario, 1 billion LLINs (i.e. an average of 250 million per year) would be required to achieve 80% of the population with access to an LLIN in the household by the end of 2017.
source: Under this scenario, we estimate that 1 billion LLINs (i.e. an average of 250 million per year) would be required to achieve 80% of the population with access to an LLIN in the household by the end of 2017, although this would only translate into 70% population use.
evidence: This is a projection based on the model analysis, shown in Figure 6.

claim: 1 billion LLINs would only translate into 70% population use under a business-as-usual scenario.
source: Under this scenario, we estimate that 1 billion LLINs (i.e. an average of 250 million per year) would be required to achieve 80% of the population with access to an LLIN in the household by the end of 2017, although this would only translate into 70% population use.
evidence: This is a projection based on the model analysis, shown in Figure 6.

claim: In a scenario with minimised over-allocation, 80% population access in 2017 would be achievable with just 700 million nets (175 million per year).
source: In a scenario with minimised over-allocation (where over allocation is set to zero), 80% population access in 2017 would be achievable with just 700 million nets (175 million per year).
evidence: This is a projection based on the model analysis, shown in Figure 6.

claim: Reducing ITN loss rate to a 3-year median retention time would have a broadly similar impact, acting in isolation, to minimising over-allocation.
source: Reducing ITN loss rate to a 3-year median retention time would have a broadly similar impact, acting in isolation, to minimising over-allocation.
evidence: This is a comparison based on the model projections shown in Figure 6.

claim: If minimised over-allocation and 3-year median retention were combined, 80% access could be reached in 2017 with around 560 million nets (140 million per year).
source: If these two hypothetical efficiency gains were combined, however, 80% access could be reached in 2017 with around 560 million nets (140 million per year).
evidence: This is a projection based on the model analysis, shown in Figure 6.

claim: The relative importance of the over-allocation and LLIN loss rates changed as more LLINs were introduced.
source: We found that the relative importance of the over-allocation and LLIN loss rates changed as more LLINs were introduced.
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis.

claim: Increasing LLIN retention times was the most important factor at low levels of net delivery.
source: Increasing LLIN retention times was the most important factor at low levels of net delivery, but as more and more nets were provided, over-allocation became progressively more important.
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis.

claim: As more and more nets were provided, over-allocation became progressively more important.
source: Increasing LLIN retention times was the most important factor at low levels of net delivery, but as more and more nets were provided, over-allocation became progressively more important.
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis.

claim: Under current levels of over-allocation and net loss, 920 million new LLINs would translate into 77% access (among those populations targeted by countries for ITN coverage) by the end of 2017.
source: Under current levels of over-allocation and net loss, we estimate that by the end of 2017 this quantity of new LLINs would translate into 77% access (among those populations targeted by countries for ITN coverage) and, assuming current behaviour patterns continue, 68% sleeping under an ITN.
evidence: This is a projection based on the model analysis, shown in Figure 6.

claim: Under current levels of over-allocation and net loss, 920 million new LLINs would translate into 68% sleeping under an ITN by the end of 2017.
source: Under current levels of over-allocation and net loss, we estimate that by the end of 2017 this quantity of new LLINs would translate into 77% access (among those populations targeted by countries for ITN coverage) and, assuming current behaviour patterns continue, 68% sleeping under an ITN.
evidence: This is a projection based on the model analysis, shown in Figure 6.

claim: Under the combined efficiency scenario with minimised over-allocation and 3-yr median ITN retention time, the 920 million nets would approach universal access (slightly over 95%).
source: Under the combined efficiency scenario with minimised over-allocation and 3-yr median ITN retention time, however, the 920 million nets would approach universal access (slightly over 95%).
evidence: This is a projection based on the model analysis, shown in Figure 6.

claim: While gains in ITN coverage have been impressive, there remains an enormous challenge if the goal of universal access is to be achieved and sustained.
source: Our results reinforce a simple message: while gains in ITN coverage have been impressive, there remains an enormous challenge if the goal of universal access is to be achieved and sustained.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data analysis and projections.

claim: While an encouraging two-thirds of households now own at least one ITN, less than half of these have enough to protect everyone who lives there.
source: The importance of the new expanded suite of indicators is also exemplified: while an encouraging two-thirds of households now own at least one ITN, less than half of these have enough to protect everyone who lives there.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data analysis.

claim: There is little evidence that non-use of available nets contributes substantially to low coverage levels.
source: Conversely, there is little evidence that non-use of available nets contributes substantially to low coverage levels.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: The overwhelming barrier to not sleeping under an ITN is lack of access rather than lack of use.
source: We therefore reinforce earlier studies that suggest the overwhelming barrier to not sleeping under an ITN is lack of access rather than lack of use WHO, 2013a; Eisele et al., 2009; 2011; Koenker and Kilian, 2014; Koenker et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a conclusion supported by the data analysis and citations to prior studies.

claim: Over-allocation becomes a major barrier to achieving universal coverage when levels of ITN provision are high because most new incoming nets are simply leading to surpluses in many households, while elsewhere there remains a shortfall.
source: What is certain is that over-allocation becomes a major barrier to achieving universal coverage when levels of ITN provision are high because most new incoming nets are simply leading to surpluses in many households, while elsewhere there remains a shortfall.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data analysis.

claim: LLINs may be lost from households at a substantially faster rate than is currently assumed.
source: One of the most important observations in our study is that LLINs may be lost from households at a substantially faster rate than is currently assumed.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: Longer retention times of the sort observed in some local studies are not supported by the body of evidence provided by triangulating large-scale net distributions and household survey data.
source: Importantly, we assess loss by comparing total inputs to countries (from deliveries) to total numbers in households (net crop), and so we measure real losses rather than, for example, reallocation of nets between relatives (Koenker et al., 2014). Longer retention times of the sort observed in some local studies are not supported by the body of evidence we have provided by triangulating large-scale net distributions and household survey data.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data analysis and comparison with other studies.

claim: Current RBM guidance is for mass ITN campaigns to be conducted every 3 years, complemented by continuous distribution of nets via routine channels.
source: Current RBM guidance is for mass ITN campaigns to be conducted every 3 years, complemented by continuous distribution of nets via routine channels in order to maintain coverage levels between those campaigns.
evidence: This represents established guidance from RBM.

claim: One-half of the campaign nets distributed, on average, will not be present in households just 2 years later.
source: However, whatever levels of coverage are achieved by a given campaign, we estimate that one-half of the campaign nets distributed, on average, will not be present in households just 2 years later.
evidence: This is an estimate derived from the model analysis.

claim: Routine distribution channels are not yet compensating fully for the rate of net loss, often displaying pronounced dips in coverage levels between mass campaigns.
source: Our coverage time-series for many countries suggest that routine distribution channels are not yet compensating fully for this rate of loss, often displaying pronounced dips in coverage levels between mass campaigns.
evidence: This is an observation based on the data analysis.

claim: Maintaining higher continuous coverage requires some combination of more frequent campaigns, greater ongoing distribution between campaigns, or more durable nets and improved care behaviour by users that lead to longer overall retention times.
source: Maintaining higher continuous coverage therefore clearly requires some combination of more frequent campaigns, greater ongoing distribution between campaigns, or more durable nets and improved care behaviour by users that lead to longer overall retention times.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data analysis and understanding of the system.

claim: Estimates of 'coverage' would be revised downwards if additional measures of net efficacy were included.
source: We considered nets in households as simply present or absent, with no allowance for their condition. In reality, of course, nets may be retained by households (and thus 'present' in our calculations) even when they are badly torn, or have diminished insecticidal properties. As such, our estimates of 'coverage' would be revised downwards if additional measures of net efficacy were included.
evidence: This is speculation about how the results would change if different assumptions were made.

claim: True LLIN requirements are likely to be considerably larger when the more rapid rates of loss are taken into account, along with the additional effect of likely over-allocation patterns.
source: We have been able to show that true LLIN requirements are likely to be considerably larger when the more rapid rates of loss are taken into account, along with the additional effect of likely over-allocation patterns.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data analysis and projections.

claim: Under business-as-usual, the number of nets required to approach full coverage is prohibitively large.
source: Under business-as-usual, the number of nets required to approach full coverage is prohibitively large.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the model projections.

claim: The pattern of diminishing coverage returns for each dollar spent is likely to be unavoidable.
source: Given that the pattern of diminishing coverage returns for each dollar spent is likely to be unavoidable, the cost–effectiveness of pursuing universal coverage rather than a lower operational target must ultimately be weighed against alternative malaria control investments.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data analysis showing diminishing returns.

claim: The main analysis covered 40 of the 47 malaria endemic countries of sub-Saharan Africa.
source: Our main analysis covered 40 of the 47 (WHO, 2013a) malaria endemic countries of sub-Saharan Africa.
evidence: This describes the scope of the study.

claim: Six endemic countries were excluded on the basis that ITNs do not form an important part of their vector control programme: Botswana, Cape Verde, Namibia, São Tomé and Príncipe, South Africa and Swaziland.
source: We excluded six endemic countries on the basis that ITNs do not form an important part of their vector control programme, as reported by the respective NMCPs to the African Leaders Malaria Alliance, ALMA (M. Renshaw, pers. comm. 3rd August 2014). These were Botswana, Cape Verde, Namibia, São Tomé and Príncipe, South Africa and Swaziland.
evidence: This describes the study methodology and is based on information from NMCPs.

claim: Mayotte was excluded because no ITN delivery or distribution data were available.
source: We also excluded the small island nation of Mayotte, for which no ITN delivery or distribution data were available.
evidence: This describes the study methodology.

claim: All analyses were limited to those populations categorized as being at risk by NMCPs.
source: We limited all analyses to those populations categorized as being at risk by NMCPs (WHO, 2013a).
evidence: This describes the study methodology.

claim: The study made the simplifying assumption that all reported ITNs were distributed among, and owned within, households situated in malaria endemic regions.
source: When interpreting NMCP distribution and household ownership data, we made the simplifying assumption that all reported ITNs were distributed among, and owned within, households situated in malaria endemic regions (Burgert et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes a methodological assumption.

claim: A discrete time stock-and-flow model was used to represent national ITN systems.
source: Like Flaxman et al.(Flaxman et al., 2010), we represented national ITN systems using a discrete time stock-and-flow model.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach.

claim: Nets delivered to a country by manufacturers were modelled as first entering a 'country stock' compartment.
source: Nets delivered to a country by manufacturers were modelled as first entering a 'country stock' compartment (stored in-country but not yet distributed to households).
evidence: This describes the model structure.

claim: The number of nets distributed in a given year was specified as a range, with all available country stock as one extreme and the NMCP-reported value as the other.
source: To accommodate this uncertainty, we specified the number of nets distributed in a given year as a range, with all available country stock as one extreme (the maximum nets that could be delivered) and the NMCP-reported value (the assumed minimum distribution level) as the other.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach to handling uncertainty.

claim: The loss function was fitted directly to the distribution and net crop data within the stock-and-flow model itself.
source: Rather than fitting the loss function to a small external dataset, we fitted this function directly to the distribution and net crop data within the stock-and-flow model itself.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach.

claim: Loss functions were fitted on a country-by-country basis, allowed to vary through time, and defined separately for cITNs and LLINs.
source: Loss functions were fitted on a country-by-country basis, allowed to vary through time, and defined separately for cITNs and LLINs.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach.

claim: The stock-and-flow model was fitted using Bayesian inference and Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC).
source: The stock-and-flow model was fitted using Bayesian inference and Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), providing time-series estimates of national household net crop for cITNs and LLINs in each country along with evaluation of under-distribution, all with posterior credible intervals.
evidence: This describes the statistical methodology.

claim: A more even distribution of nets yields a greater proportion of households owning nets than if those same nets are concentrated in fewer households.
source: In simple terms, a more even distribution yields a greater proportion of households owning nets than if those same nets are concentrated in fewer households.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the relationship between distribution patterns and coverage.

claim: Histograms for different countries vary in a broadly predictable way according to national net crop.
source: By analysing such data from multiple surveys, previous studies have demonstrated that histograms for different countries vary in a broadly predictable way according to national net crop (Flaxman et al., 2010; Yukich et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Household size strongly influences the relationship between net crop and household ownership distribution.
source: One aspect that is known to strongly influence the relationship between net crop and household ownership distribution is the size of households found in different countries (Networks, 2014; Yukich et al., 2013), which varies greatly across sub-Saharan Africa (Swaziland, for example has an average household size of around three members, while in Senegal the average is nearly ten).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and examples.

claim: Household size varies greatly across sub-Saharan Africa, with Swaziland having an average household size of around three members, while in Senegal the average is nearly ten.
source: One aspect that is known to strongly influence the relationship between net crop and household ownership distribution is the size of households found in different countries (Networks, 2014; Yukich et al., 2013), which varies greatly across sub-Saharan Africa (Swaziland, for example has an average household size of around three members, while in Senegal the average is nearly ten).
evidence: This claim provides specific examples from the data.

claim: The study used a bivariate histogram model to link net crop to ownership distributions for each household size stratum.
source: We extended earlier analyses (Flaxman et al., 2010; Yukich et al., 2013) to explicitly account for household size: using a bivariate (i.e. two- rather than one-dimensional) histogram model to link net crop to ownership distributions for each household size stratum (see Supplementary Information).
evidence: This describes the methodological approach.

claim: The negative binomial distribution was replaced with a 2-d zero-truncated Poisson distribution.
source: We replaced the negative binomial distribution with a 2-d zero-truncated Poisson distribution and, for each household size stratum, fitted the distribution using two parameters: (i) the proportion of households with zero ITNs and (ii) the mean number of ITNs per ITN-owning household.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach.

claim: Both parameters (proportion of households with zero ITNs and mean number of ITNs per ITN-owning household) were strongly related to national net crop.
source: Using the household-level data from 83 national surveys, we found that both parameters were strongly related to national net crop, allowing bivariate histograms to be generated for every country-year that were closely representative of the true ITN ownership distribution.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: The distribution of net ownership tended to vary substantially between households of different sizes within a given country.
source: First, the distribution of net ownership tended to vary substantially between households of different sizes within a given country and this variation would be missed if all households were considered together.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: All else being equal, larger households would be expected to own more nets than smaller ones.
source: This makes sense: all else being equal, larger households would be expected to own more nets than smaller ones and so distribution patterns would differ systematically.
evidence: This is a logical inference about household net ownership patterns.

claim: ITN use is less directly linked to national net crop and is primarily determined by the availability of nets within households.
source: We took a different approach for the final indicator, % population who slept under an ITN the previous night. ITN use is less directly linked to national net crop and is primarily determined by the availability of nets within households (Eisele et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and represents understanding of the relationship between access and use.

claim: % population with access to an ITN within their household displayed the largest correlation with ITN use (adjusted R2= 0.96).
source: A total of 83 of the 102 national surveys contained data allowing the relationship to be explored between ITN use and each of the three access indicators with, perhaps unsurprisingly, % population with access to an ITN within their household displaying the largest correlation (adjusted R2= 0.96).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: The study used a simple Bayesian regression model to predict time-series of the ITN use indicator for every country.
source: We fitted this relationship across the 83 surveys using a simple Bayesian regression model (see Supplementary Information) and used it to predict time-series of the ITN use indicator for every country.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach.

claim: The current needs assessment exercise is designed to identify the number of LLINs required to achieve coverage targets by 2017.
source: The current needs assessment exercise that countries are undertaking (RBM-HWG, 2014; RBM, 2014) is designed to identify the number of LLINs required to achieve coverage targets by 2017.
evidence: This describes the purpose of the RBM-HWG needs assessment, supported by citations.

claim: Two of the 40 endemic countries in the study did not participate in the RBM-HWG needs assessment exercise (Djibouti and Equatorial Guinea).
source: We then generalized this experiment to predict the likely level of coverage (for all four indicators) achievable by 2017 under a broad spectrum of LLIN delivery levels, equivalent to a total for sub-Saharan Africa (two of the 40 endemic countries in our study did not participate in the RBM-HWG needs assessment exercise [Djibouti and Equatorial Guinea], and so our scenario analysis is based on the set of 38 remaining countries; to maintain comparability through time, we combined needs assessment data for mainland Tanzania and Zanzibar, and for Sudan and South Sudan) of between zero and 2.5 billion nets across the 4-year period.
evidence: This describes the scope of the scenario analysis.

claim: In 2013, 21% (17%–26%) of ITNs were over-allocated.
source: We estimated that, in 2013, 21% (17%–26%) of ITNs were over-allocated and this has worsened over time as overall net provision has increased.
evidence: This is an estimate derived from the model analysis.

claim: Over-allocation has worsened over time as overall net provision has increased.
source: We estimated that, in 2013, 21% (17%–26%) of ITNs were over-allocated and this has worsened over time as overall net provision has increased.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: Rates of ITN loss from households are more rapid than previously thought, with 50% lost after 23 (20–28) months.
source: We estimated that rates of ITN loss from households are more rapid than previously thought, with 50% lost after 23 (20–28) months.
evidence: This is an estimate derived from the model analysis.

claim: The current estimate of 920 million additional ITNs required to achieve universal coverage would in reality yield a lower level of coverage (77% population access).
source: We predict that the current estimate of 920 million additional ITNs required to achieve universal coverage would in reality yield a lower level of coverage (77% population access).
evidence: This is a prediction based on the model analysis.

claim: By improving efficiency, the 920 million ITNs could yield population access as high as 95%.
source: By improving efficiency, however, the 920 million ITNs could yield population access as high as 95%.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the model analysis under improved efficiency scenarios.

claim: All four ITN indicators show very low coverage levels and modest year-on-year increases for the first 5 years from 2000, with a marked inflexion point in 2005 and much more rapid gains thereafter.
source: All four indicators show a similar temporal trend: very low coverage levels and modest year-on-year increases for the first 5 years from 2000, with a marked inflexion point in 2005 and much more rapid gains thereafter.
evidence: This is an observation based on the data shown in Figure 2.

claim: All four indicators show that the pace of increase has, overall, slowed since 2005.
source: Importantly, however, all four indicators show that the pace of increase has, overall, slowed since 2005.
evidence: This is an observation based on the data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Manufacturer data on deliveries were available for LLINs only.
source: Manufacturer data on deliveries were available for LLINs only.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the available data, as noted in Figure 1.

claim: The study used data from 102 national surveys.
source: We developed a Bayesian model using data from 102 national surveys, triangulated against delivery data and distribution reports, to generate year-by-year estimates of four ITN coverage indicators.
evidence: This describes the data used in the study.
